en: The Ritual for the Samādhi of the Dhāraṇī for Subduing Poisonous Harm Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
following the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* Repentance Ritual,
composed by the Song Dynasty Dongshan Śramaṇa Zunshe at Tiantai Guo.
Revised at the Hermitage on Mount Dailai in Siming; Second Revision. First: Preface to the Origins of the Circumstances. Regarding this second revision, there are four causes and conditions.
First, on the day he first gathered [his disciples] for the purification of the state,
he intended to cultivate himself at Lingxu; however,
being pressed by his scheduled deadline, he hastened to achieve completion.
Within this, matters, principles, and phrasing are intermingled;
being neither sufficiently detailed nor concise, it is generally difficult to understand.
It is based on the title of the *Bai lu* (Records of Baizhang), which requests the method for the Avalokiteśvara Repentance Rite.
Regarding the current re-editing, there is a commitment to adhering to the fundamental principles.
The titles of the scriptures used for the editing and the specific texts edited shall differ from other productions;
these two together constitute the *Guoqing ji* (The Guoqing Collection).
I have excised most of the flowery rhetoric and used exclusively the terminology found in the sutras,
commentaries, *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, and *Mohe zhiguan*. Since these citations are well-established,
they serve as authoritative evidence.
This is so that future generations may increase their right faith.
Third, I have recently obtained the collection compiled by Guoqing;
as a late learner acting with rash simplicity, I have appended [this] after the texts on repentance and vows.
Furthermore, I have added the four repentances from the *Lotus Sūtra Repentance Ritual* (Fahua chanwen), along with their phonetic transcriptions and Sanskrit characters.
Additionally, I saw another manuscript that had deleted the various ritual procedures as well as the texts concerning contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*),
writing down only the ranks of the Buddhas and the repentances and vows.
The title reads "Text for the Liturgy of Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, one manuscript appears to have been transcribed in old age;
entire lines have been omitted, and the main text and the marginal annotations are indistinguishable from one another.
I have instead privately added annotations within the lines,
intending to distinguish those who would harm such people by taking up and discarding [the teachings] based merely on their superficial appeal without proper study.
To destroy the gateway to the nectar of immortality brings consequences that are no small matter.
Now, by revising this once more, I seek to distance myself from all such faults.
Fourth, I have taken all the various passages concerning contemplative wisdom and placed them after the narrative events.
This ensures that the application of mindfulness is thorough and complete,
so that practitioners do not waste their efforts in vain.
One should know that the three types of repentance in the Mahāyāna must take rational contemplation as their primary focus.
The *Zhiguan* states:
"The foundation of contemplative wisdom must not be lacking.
The *Fuxing* commentary explains:
This is because if one lacks the wisdom of contemplation, ascetic practices will result in nothing but fruitless suffering.
The *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* states:
"All Mahāyāna sūtras clarify the methods for repentance."
All of these take this contemplation as their core.
If one departs from this contemplation,
it cannot be called the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Repentance.
The *Buzhi yi* (Supplementary Ritual Manual) states:
"As for the method of ritual repentance (*li chan fa*),
although the world alike studies its ceremonial procedures,"
One's mental cultivation is often incomplete;
perhaps one has merely read the texts of repentance and does not fully master them,
or perhaps one uses forceful suppression to resist conceptual observation.
Lacking the wind of diligent exertion and missing the sequence of the gateway,
it is said that the arduous practice of asceticism is not the cause of Nirvana;
this is precisely where the clear admonition of our Grandfather, the Great Physician, resides.
The preceding four points correspond to the four *siddhāntas*.
This concludes the exposition on causes and conditions. 2.
Clarifying the Primary Intention. *Commentary on the "Sutra of the Avalokiteśvara Dharani Requested by the Bodhisattva"* (Second).
As before, according to the person’s capacity, clarify the method through ten points:
first, purify the ritual site; second, perform prostrations;
third, burn incense and scatter flowers; fourth, focus the mind and practice counting the breaths.
1. Prepare five sets of tooth-sticks and pure water; 2. Invite the Triple Gem;
3. Recite mantras; 4. Confess one's transgressions;
5. Prostrate; 6. Practice seated meditation.
The *Shu* (Commentary) merely explains the sutras and does not have the leisure to set forth the methods in detail;
therefore, it has simply followed the traditional listings.
Since the *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters) already correctly clarifies the ritual procedures for specific affairs.
The intent of this differs slightly from that of the older traditions.
In the "Five Essentials," the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) is listed sixth,
whereas in the *Baolu* (Record of the Hundred), following the sutras, the tooth-stick is placed after the invitation to the Sage.
In the old tradition, ten types of seated meditation were recorded,
but in the *Baolu*, these were changed to recitation of sutras;
thus, the fourth type, counting the breath, was taken as the practice of dhyāna.
Formerly, because sitting in meditation was emphasized, the chanting and recitation were neglected.
Therefore, although the current number of items is ten, they are exclusively based on the *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters) as the standard.
Nevertheless, these ten points—
Each possesses both phenomena and principle, all of which are universally connected to response and stimulus;
they collectively pervade the three karmas,
completely purify the three obstacles, and fully harmonize with the three virtues.
How straightforward is the essential path to liberation!
Thus, in terms of phenomena, it consists of the ten categories of current ritual practices;
in terms of principle, it is simply twofold.
First, the correct contemplation of the Middle Way within the *Anulomā-dhāraṇī*;
second, the cultivation of contemplation through successive practices.
These matters and principles necessarily rely upon the three karmas.
The principle by which the three karmas form the spiritual capacity (ki) is such that there is nothing to which it does not correspond.
Correspondence is the purification of karma; the purification of karma is the removal of hindrances;
and the removal of hindrances is the realization of virtue.
When one realizes virtue, there is neither principle nor phenomenon, nor is there any response or stimulus;
all is utterly tranquil—so who would discuss the ten intentions?
[One must] first purify the site of practice before being able to prepare for them.
It may be appropriate for the "pervasive" (tong) to encompass both phenomena and principle;
however, why does the text immediately discuss "response and resonance" (ganying) and even "converging virtues"?
The answer is that these ten points are established according to their specific distinctions.
There is no lack of distinction between skillful means and correct cultivation;
now, speaking in general terms,
since it is granted that both phenomena and principle are fully present.
Why should one doubt the response of the sacred?
Furthermore, all invocations of the sages are based upon three principles.
First, the marking of the mind; second, practice; third, realization.
Setting aside for a moment the preparation of the *maṇḍala*, what is it that one seeks by marking the mind through various categories?
If the purity of the three karmas brings results even when not yet timely, how much more so when within the *maṇḍala*?
Throughout his successive encounters with events, he contemplated the principles until their meaning was realized as if through direct verification.
Since his three requests were fulfilled, how could there not have been a corresponding response?
If this was so even at the site of enlightenment, it may be known that it was likewise so in the other nine places.
Furthermore, I shall cite scriptures to provide corroborating evidence for these ten points.
Regarding "resonance and response" and so forth, the Sūtra says:
"You should now prostrate yourself with your five limbs touching the ground."
While burning incense, scattering flowers, and fixing the mind on counting the breaths,
one should, for the sake of all sentient beings, invoke that Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas.
As these words were being spoken, [the Buddhas appeared].
Both the Buddha and the bodhisattvas arrived together in this country;
however, this was merely the Sage’s demonstration of the method for making an invitation,
and no actual practice had yet been undertaken.
He merely said, "When these words were spoken, the Buddha and the others had already descended.
Were it not for the power of my three requests, how could they have been brought here?
He prostrated himself on the ground to offer homage for a second time.
The remaining proofs concern the three intentions beginning with "requesting" (adhyeṣaṇā).
Furthermore, the fact that the people of the country personally offer tooth-sticks and pure water serves as proof for the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) and the sixth intention.
The three mantras all state that one sees the Buddha manifest before one;
this attests to the intent of reciting the mantras.
Throughout various texts, there are passages concerning the removal of obstacles and the vision of the Buddha.
Śāriputra explained his intention:
"If one hears this sutra and receives, maintains, reads, recites, and so forth,
they will immediately transcend the offenses of birth and death for immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
This explains the intent of the recitation.
When these ten intents are complete and perfected, the response will be manifest;
let the practitioner contemplate this.
Since these ten points from beginning to end have already exhausted the three karmas,
let them not be spent in vain;
always remember with sorrow the blood-stained weeping of Vaidehī as she struck her head in supplication.
This is also clear evidence of the responsive resonance between the first two intentions mentioned above;
the rest may be understood by analogy.
Why, then, do ordinary practitioners establish *maṇḍalas* in a manner that is indistinguishable from mundane affairs?
On the contrary, this will invite karmic entanglements and make it extremely difficult to eliminate obstacles;
this is as condemned in the *Fuxing ji* (Record of Aiding Practice).
As for the actual cultivation:
One must broaden the mind to encompass far-reaching matters and clarify both principle and phenomena.
If one has not yet attained this understanding oneself, one should consult those who do.
As the Book of Documents says: "Those who act on their own are small; do not employ what you have not consulted."
The ten intentions shall now be explained.
1. Adorning the Bodhimanda: The *First Adornment of the Bodhimanda* (Dàochǎng dìyī zhuāngyán) states in the *Bǎilù*:
"One should adorn and decorate the bodhimanda."
The ground was smeared with fragrant mud,
and various banners and canopies were suspended.
An image of the Buddha was installed facing south, while an image of Avalokiteśvara was separately placed facing east.
The *Zhiguan* states:
"In a pure place or a ritual site (*maṇḍala*),
invite images of Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
In the Western Dharma-hall, one must place an image of Avalokiteśvara facing east;
on his right shoulder, place Akṣobhya;
and on his left shoulder, facing south, place an image of the Buddha.
Within this, it is not improper to further install Śākyamuni.
Once the adornments are fully prepared, one should then install the image, set out the ritual staff (*yaṣṭi*), and pure water.
When attending to the calls of nature, one should apply ash to the body on both sides.
Having bathed for purification and donned new, clean robes,
the *Baolu* states: "When the ten practitioners have returned,
they should sit upon the ground facing west."
If the ground is low and damp, place a low-legged bed upon it.
One should offer worship with all one's strength every day;
if one cannot provide for this, there must be no lack of offering on the first day.
The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) states:
"Although sincerity of body and speech must be supplemented by the assistance of merit,
those who perform this daily do so with even greater efficacy."
Fearing that my strength may not suffice, I shall follow from the first day.
I must first apply my own wealth and resources to the utmost extent of my ability;
for one hundred cycles, I shall observe the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* for twenty-one days.
Regarding the practice of observing this sutra for seven periods of seven days,
beginning entirely on days of fasting (*upoṣadha*) to establish the fundamental contemplation,
the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says:
Regarding the practice of meditation through successive stages based on the sacred image and ritual implements,
the *Zhi guan* states:
"The site of practice (*daochang*) is the realm of purity."
This treats the husks of the five stages to reveal the rice of the true mark;
it is also the application of meditative concentration and wisdom to adorn the Dharma-body.
(From the *Fuxing*)
The site is that which is adorned.
Although the means of adornment are many, they do not transcend meditative concentration and wisdom.
Although the offerings are numerous, they do not transcend the moving and the unmoving.
The *Zhiguan* states:
"Fragrant mud is none other than the unsurpassed śīla.
The *Fuxing* says:
The ultimate fragrance of the precepts thoroughly anoints the reality of the true principle.
Regarding the banners and canopies,
the *Zhiguan* says:
"Banner" (fan) means "to overturn.
It refers to overturning the deluded, arising, and active movements within the Dharma-realm to produce understanding.
As for "canopy" (gai):
Contemplating the five aggregates as being like the binding of a rabbit, one gives rise to great compassion that covers the entire dharma-realm.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "Contemplating that the aggregates are fundamentally empty is like the binding of a rabbit."
Because the cloud of non-referential compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) pervades the entire dharma-realm, it is so called.
Furthermore, regarding "the place of tranquility" (*śānta-sthāna*):
according to *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, being far removed from the two extremes is designated as "tranquility."
As for "abiding" (*sthāna*),
the principle of truth is the abiding;
this is because the Dharma of the Middle Way is profound, remote, and deep.
Regarding the image of Amitābha and others, the Commentary states:
"The image of Amitābha represents the realm of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and true reality (dharmatā);
Avalokiteśvara represents the wisdom of the Middle Way and correct contemplation."
The Great Power represents the cultivation of the spiritual power of merit.
As for the West:
in relation to the Five Elements, the West corresponds to Metal.
The principle of decisive and upright judgment corresponds to the Truth of the Path among the Four Noble Truths.
"Path" (mārga) is so named because it is that which enables passage;
for by means of wisdom, one perceives the underlying principle.
The Greatly Wise Avalokiteśvara can eliminate and subdue poison and harm.
Regarding those who enter and exit from the left and right:
the left symbolizes meditative concentration, while exiting signifies dispersal.
Because concentration is used to still distraction, one must exit from the left;
the right represents the provisional (upāya) and the left represents the real (bhūta).
Because one enters the real by means of the provisional, one must enter from the right.
Regarding "bathing":
through śamatha and vipaśyanā, one cultivates true contemplation to wash away hindrances and purify wisdom.
The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) says:
That which is eliminated is like delusion; that which can wash it away is like the sun’s observation.
Because the body is free from defilement, both subject and object are pure.
Furthermore, the aids to the path are like the application of ash.
Right contemplation is like clear water;
it thoroughly cleanses the impurities upon the body.
As for the new, clean garment:
The *Bai lu* states that the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*) covers the ugliness of the two extremes.
The *Fuxing yu* says:
Quiescent patience accords with the essence [of reality], like clothing upon the body.
Question: Why is there no contemplative understanding regarding the functions of excretion and urination? Answer:
However, these activities of excretion, urination, eating, and drinking are not governed by the principles of samādhi practice.
Therefore, there is no explanation for the text.
If one were to perform contemplation, what harm would there be?
It is as in the text of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, when defecating or urinating, one should form the mental image of following the natural course of the channels;
by thus washing away filth and impurities, one returns to a state of purity.
As for the remaining texts, they are not established as permanent rules.
You may perform these contemplations as you wish;
simply ensure they accord with the perfect and correct aids and are in elegant conformity with the Dharma-characteristics, which I shall set forth in detail later.
2. The Second Method for Performing Prostrations. The *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Items) states:
Each person should hold an incense burner and, with single-minded devotion, prostrate themselves with the five limbs touching the ground toward the western direction.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "One who clearly understands the sounds should chant [this],
prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground."
In principle, one must first approach with both knees on the ground and then extend both elbows;
subsequently, one should touch the forehead to the ground, letting the liver and gallbladder (the torso) lie flat.
One should visualize the Buddha’s feet and place one's hands beneath them to support them, as if facing him directly before one's eyes.
The Commentary states: "The Great Sage constantly desires to rescue and deliver those who are without sores;
because poison cannot enter them, he causes the three karmas to serve as the pivot for understanding the principle.
The Commentary further states: "The ground is the ground of the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*)."
If the mind is conjoined with that which corresponds to sarvajñā (all-knowledge),
it is called "prostrating on the ground.
If one is separated from sarvajñā and gives rise to the five aggregates, [it is not so].
This is merely lying flat;
it does not eliminate poison and harm, and one remains submerged in birth and death.
Now, the five limbs clarify the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The left foot is form (rūpa);
the right foot is feeling (vedanā);
the left hand is volitional formations (saṃskāra).
The right hand is volition;
the head is consciousness. Why is this so?
Precepts are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
Their unmanifest nature is subtle and hidden like the primary elements;
it represents the left foot.
Samādhi is that which receives;
samādhi is the dharma of the mind-spirit and is yang.
It represents the right foot.
Perception (saṃjñā) is like the yang, as it investigates external objects during the day;
it represents the right hand.
Volition (cetanā), which is the mental factor of intention, is like the yin.
The "manifestation" (vijñapti) represents the left hand.
Since the five consciousnesses reside in the head and are capable of discernment,
consciousness is correlated with the head.
If one relies on the stage of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge),
one attains the precepts of the fivefold dharma-body,
because these protect and guard the seven branches [of bodily and vocal action].
This aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is definitively the right reception of samādhi;
this aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha) is wisdom;
and this awakening to the knowledge of emptiness is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha).
Liberation is the practice;
practice can bring about entanglement.
Because liberation is free from entanglement, it is contrasted with the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
The knowledge and vision of liberation is the aggregate of consciousness,
because it is capable of discerning;
with the fivefold Dharma-body, one strikes down the five aggregates of birth and death.
The Sūtra says:
"By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
Therefore, it is called "prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground.
By causing poison and harm to be extinguished and subdued,
one is then born beyond birth-and-death, transcending all worldly burdens with ease.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to our Teacher, Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Amitāyus, the World-Honored One of the Western Quarter.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Seven Buddhas of the Past, the World-Honored Ones.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the *dhāraṇī* for subduing and eliminating poisonous harm, the *dhāraṇī* for destroying obstacles of evil karma, and the *dhāraṇī* of the six-syllable phrase.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Honored Ones of the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Sangha of noble Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, such as Śāriputra and others.
When performing prostrations to the Buddha, one should contemplate: "The nature of both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent;
the mutual resonance of this spiritual response is inconceivable."
In this place of my practice, like the reflection of Śākyamuni appearing within a sovereign wish-fulfilling jewel,
my own form appears before Śākyamuni; with my head meeting his feet face-to-face, I take refuge and pay homage.
When performing prostrations to Amitāyus Buddha, one says: "Amitāyus Buddha appears as a reflection," and so forth. Regarding the method of visualization for the prostration:
"The Dharma-nature of true emptiness is like space;
the eternally abiding Dharma-treasure is inconceivable. My own body’s shadow appears before this Dharma-treasure."
There are none who do not take refuge in and pay homage to the Sangha;
the procedure for this is the same as the aforementioned ritual for paying homage to the Buddha, with the only modification being that one pays homage to the Bodhisattvas.

Specifically, when paying homage to Avalokiteśvara, one should state: "In order to seek the extinction of hindrances, I prostrate at your feet. This is the core of the rite of repentance; it specifically requires three prostrations to symbolize the breaking of the three obstacles, as well as to express diligence and respect.
3. Burning Incense and Scattering Flowers, Part Three. Regarding "Burning Incense and Scattering Flowers," the *Zhiguan* states: "Burn incense and direct the mind to offer the three karmas.
The *Fuxing* commentary explains: "The 'three karmas' refer to the offerings of body, speech, and mind."
With the body kneeling upright, the mouth recites aloud, and the mind performs visualization.
The *Bai lu* states: "When the prostrations are finished, burn incense, scatter flowers, and speak these words:
'All these assemblies...'"
Each person knelt on their right knee,
reverently holding incense and flowers,
making offerings according to the Dharma.
Making offerings to the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma realm; at this point,
holding incense and flowers, one should contemplate as follows:
May these incense and flowers pervade the ten directions as a subtle and wondrous pavilion of light,
with celestial music and divine precious incense.
The celestial delicacies, divine jeweled robes,
and inconceivable wondrous dharma-dusts—
each and every particle of dust produces all other particles.
From each and every atom, all phenomena emerge,
revolving without obstruction, mutually adorning one another,
and pervading everywhere before the Triple Gem in the ten directions.
Before the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm,
my body is present in every place,
performing offerings that pervade the whole of the Dharma-realm.
In each and every place, without confusion or obstruction,
they perform the work of Buddhas until the end of the future,
universally perfuming all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
Having visualized that all who have been perfumed by these [emanations] give rise to the bodhicitta and enter together into the non-arising realization of Buddha-wisdom,
one scatters flowers, takes up the incense burner once more, and utters these sincere words:
May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the realms of the ten directions,
making offerings to all Buddhas.
The Honored Ones, the various Bodhisattvas,
and the immeasurable assembly of Śrāvakas,
by means of this arising light-pavilion, [manifested their presence].
Transcending boundless limits,
throughout infinite Buddha-fields,
they perform the work of Buddhas.
It universally perfumes all sentient beings,
causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Having arisen, one performs a single prostration and folds away the sitting mat.

Regarding "understanding," the sub-commentary says:
Incense is fragrant and aromatic, masking foul odors;
it symbolizes wisdom that severs the fetters.
Incense is, indeed, wisdom.
It is also called "stopping goodness" (*śamatha-kuśala*).
Flowers can adorn and manifest meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
concentration is the adornment of merit (*puṇya-vyūha*).
It is also called "practicing goodness.
Furthermore, the flower symbolizes wisdom;
as a visible phenomenon, the flower stands in contrast to wisdom.
This is the meaning of illuminating and clearly perceiving principle.
Incense serves to symbolize meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
incense, through its subtle permeation, corresponds to concentration.
Regarding the meaning of "quiescence," this mutual correspondence clarifies that within wisdom there is concentration,
and within concentration there is wisdom.
To clarify further, each possesses both concentration and wisdom.
Furthermore, fragrance corresponds to unmanifest wholesome action;
this unmanifest arises based on manifest action as its cause.
However, it must further function spontaneously and arise continuously;
just as when incense is burned, fire serves as the condition,
whereby the incense smoke then spontaneously pervades everywhere.
Flowers respond by performing wholesome deeds;
if one does not perform wholesome deeds, they will not arise.
It is like scattering fragrant flowers with the hands.
If one does not move the flower, it will not scatter.
By employing these ten types of practitioners,
one clarifies the intent of subduing and eliminating [afflictions].
4. Counting the Breaths with Fixed Mindfulness, Part Four. The *Bai lu* (One Hundred Records) states:
One should face west and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), fixing the mind on the counting of breaths so that the mind does not become distracted.
Do not frequently pant or gasp for breath;
for the sake of sentient beings, remain [in meditation] for the duration of ten recitations.
The commentary states that ten breaths constitute one recitation.
One hundred breaths constitute ten recitations (*daśa-smṛti*).
The *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Upon first reaching the meditation seat, one should sit in a stable and comfortable manner."
If one wishes to sit in the half-lotus posture, place the left foot upon the right thigh,
drawing it close to the body so that the toes are level with the left and right thighs respectively.
If performing the full [posture], place the right foot upon the left thigh;
then, place the left palm upon the right palm and set it firmly against the body at the level of the heart.
Keeping the body upright and straight, align the nose with the navel.
Sit facing forward on a level surface with the mouth closed;
let the lips and teeth just barely touch, and extend the tongue toward the palate.
Closing the eyes merely serves to cut off external light.
As for "breath" (*śvāsa*):
when it has sound, it is called "wind" (*vāyu*).
Obstruction is called "labored breathing" (chuan).
Non-obstruction is called "knotting" (jie).
It is neither sounding nor knotted, neither coarse nor rough, nor slippery.
The inhalation and exhalation are continuous, as if existing and yet as if non-existent.
When the spirit is supported and settled in tranquility, it is called "breath" (*xi*).
By guarding against the scattering of wind and the stagnation of panting, the vital energy and momentum become stilled and settled.
The *Bai lu* states:
"Once the ten recitations are completed, one next contemplates the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions."
The wondrous body of true reality is like empty space.
Furthermore, one should maintain loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
when forming this thought, it is as if one were in the first dhyāna.
The *Shuchao* states: "Having maintained mindfulness for a long duration, one awakens calmly and gradually.
This 'binding of mindfulness' is an exhortation to engage the mental faculty (*manas-karma*) in silent recitation;
even those of inferior capacity can thereby attain concentration of mind and the cessation of distraction."
Those of medium capacity immediately attain subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-vihāra*);
those of superior capacity immediately attain the concentration of the stage of "not yet arrived" (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
This is the joy that gives rise to the various dhyānas and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states.
The Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions and all meditative concentrations are, in this context, the ten recollections applied to ten types of practitioners;
these differ according to whether one practices counting the breath or restraining the mind. If the counting of the breath is properly adjusted, [the practice succeeds].
When body and mind are tranquil and the four great elements are in harmony,
one immediately subdues and eliminates the poisonous harms of karmic retribution. If,
while counting the breaths, one develops a virtuous mind, [the same occurs].
When both evil karma and worldly virtues are stilled,
one breathes with the count of humans and devas.
If one contemplates that this breath is wind-energy, then wind is form (*rūpa*).
One is able to observe that the mind-king is consciousness,
which experiences this breath;
the mental application directed toward this breath is perception, and all other factors are formations.
The breath possessing the five aggregates is the four foundations of mindfulness;
this is called the breath of the śrāvaka.
If one contemplates that the past breath was caused by ignorance, [this is the breath of the bodhisattva].
The cessation that constitutes the present retribution of the causal conditions of the three periods of time is the cessation of the pratyekabuddha.
If one contemplates this cessation as neither preserving nor clinging to it, that is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
The non-arising of unwholesome states is called *śīla* (morality).
Enduring these occurrences is called *kṣānti* (patience).
The continuous succession of moments is called *vīrya* (diligence).
Knowing the count without confusion is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Illuminating and discerning whether the breath is deviant or correct is wisdom (*prajñā*).
The completion of these six perfections brings rest.
If one contemplates the breath as achieving the wisdom of signlessness,
it is called the breath of the Shared Teaching;
if one contemplates the breath as the Middle Way Buddha-nature, which is neither empty nor mundane.
The practice of contemplating the breath sequentially from beginning to end is termed the Separate Teaching (biejiao) method of calming the breath.
If one contemplates this breath through the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), it is the three truths within a single mind,
without sequential stages or before-and-after.
This is called the cessation of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Regarding "the practitioner of Buddha-recitation," the scriptural text instructs one to recite the names of the Seven Buddhas and so forth.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states:
"All dharmas are from the beginning without arising and without ceasing;
because the Bodhisattva believes and delights in the two bodies of form and dharma as being like empty space."
One attains non-obstruction in all places.
What is called "obstruction" refers to things such as Mount Sumeru.
This person has not yet attained the divine eye;
yet by recollecting the Buddhas of other directions,
they attain the dharma of meditative concentration and see the Buddhas according to their mental vision.
One should also carefully analyze this according to ten modes of manifestation.
The commentary states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions are themselves the ten dharma-realms."
All possess Buddha-nature.
The seven Buddhas are the seven factors of enlightenment.
For those who contemplate birth after birth, it is appropriate to take the four truths as their object and give rise to compassion as their means.
The text is extensive and not cited here; it may be understood through reflection.
One should know that one must maintain focused mindfulness and not allow the mind to become lax;
this is merely for the purpose of collecting the thoughts. Furthermore, one must recognize that the faculties and dispositions of practitioners differ.
During the twenty-one days, or even the forty-nine days, there were those who experienced profound spiritual awakenings.
Therefore, in the commentary (*shu*), the author extensively discusses the three faculties and ten types of practitioners to clarify their respective manifestations,
so that the underlying intent may be understood in its full depth.
The practitioner reflects deeply.
Just as it is with the counting of breaths, so it is with all other gates;
each is applied according to the ten types of practitioners.
This clarifies the intention for subduing and eliminating [obstacles].
5. Regarding the fifth, the *Zhaoqing shu* (Explanatory Text on Invocation) states:
"Invocation has three meanings."
First is requesting for oneself;
second is requesting for others;
third is requesting to protect the true Dharma.
One who requests [the Dharma] for oneself is like Sūnata;
one who acts for others is like Candracchattra;
one who protects the Dharma is like the seven-word verse.
Vowing for oneself is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas;
acting for the sake of others is the precept of gathering sentient beings;
and protecting the Dharma is the precept of gathering the true Dharma.
The three points of mastery are in fact one: to cause one's own precepts,
concentration, and wisdom to be bright and pure is precisely what constitutes the gathering of wholesome dharmas.
Benefiting others through one's own self encompasses all sentient beings.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Now, we shall examine the practitioner’s deviations and correctness.
Alternatively, one may consider oneself as the primary [object of protection] and others as secondary;
this applies likewise even to the protection of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are three ways of making such a request for oneself.
"Inviting" (*yān*), "supplicating" (*qǐqìng*), and "requesting" (*yuànqǐng*)—these three are also for the purpose of protecting others' Dharma.
"Inviting" (*yán*) carries the meaning of bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up; it refers to the act of drawing [the deity] forth and corresponds to bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Prostration with the five limbs touching the ground is an example of this.
To pray is to initiate [the act], while to seek earnestly through speech is verbal karma;
the four-line verse is an example of this.
The aspiration is precisely the locus of the essential mind;
it is the very act of binding one's mindfulness.
Although this may be the case when applied specifically to individual cases, in general, all [factors] must be present.
The combined practice of the three karmas should be performed with a state of mental mastery;
the present meaning requires that one extend an invitation [to the deities].
The *Bai lu* (Records of the Hundred) says:
Have one person prepare the incense and lamps;
each person kneels in turn to perform the invocation.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says:
Regarding the ritual of mutual kneeling:
the three points are raised and prominent;
the body is bent, and the palms are joined.
Their eyes are fixed upon the golden countenance;
yet in recent times, morals have become diluted and corrupt,
such that there is no longer any sign of prostration.
The banner of pride remains unbroken;
the ocean of karma is difficult to overturn;
one still lets loose this defiled body.
Rest securely in the Great Way;
look upon these clear admonitions with earnest diligence.

Recite as follows: "I single-mindedly entreat: Namo to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni, World-Honored One. (Recite this three times. Having invited the Three Jewels previously venerated, the invocation for the Buddha is recited as follows: "My three karmas are by nature like empty space; The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is likewise so. Without departing from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) for the sake of sentient beings, He comes together with the assembly to receive this offering. The invocation for the Dharma is recited as follows: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like space and cannot be seen."

The eternally abiding Dharma Jewel is inconceivable; I now entreat it with my three karmas according to the Dharma. I only pray that you will manifest yourself to accept this offering; The invitation to the Sangha is the same as the previous invitation to the Buddha.
The only difference is that the titles have been changed.
In various versions of the ritual for repentance (*chánfǎ*),
verses are recited to praise the Buddha following the invocation.
This repentance liturgy lacks a text for praise;
I have now recorded these verses from the *Sutra of the Threefold Invocation of Avalokiteśvara* and published them here.
The Greatly Compassionate One of Great Renown, the Auspicious One who brings peace and happiness,
always speaks auspicious words. For those beings in extreme suffering,
if they hear his name, they shall be freed from suffering and attain liberation.
They also sport within the hells, taking upon themselves suffering out of great compassion;
or dwelling among the animals, they manifest in animal forms to teach them with great wisdom,
causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind.
Sometimes dwelling among the asuras, he tames their minds with gentle words to eliminate the habit of arrogance;
swiftly reaching the shore of the unconditioned,
he manifests as a hungry ghost, from whose hands flows fragrant, colored milk.
To those oppressed by hunger and thirst, he gives so that they may attain full satisfaction;
with a heart of great loving-kindness and great compassion, he sports within the five realms of existence,
constantly cultivating wisdom through supreme and unsurpassed skillful means.
Universally teaching all beings, causing them to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and always attain a place of peace and joy, reaching the shore of Great Nirvana;
having offered these praises, he expresses his feelings as he pleases.
6. Chapter Six: Providing Tooth-sticks and Pure Water. The *Juyangzhi Jingshui Jing* (Sutra on Providing Tooth-sticks and Pure Water) states:
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī immediately prepared tooth-sticks and pure water.
[The text] is bestowed upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Regarding *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation), it merely mentions providing willow branches and so forth, but does not state that they are bestowed;
now, following the sutra, the practitioner is instructed to kneel and bestow them.
The chant says:
"I have now prepared willow twigs and pure water; I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on me and accept them. This is recited three times.
The *Fuhangshi* (Supplementary Ritual Manual) explains:
Because Avalokiteśvara holds a willow branch in his left hand and carries a water flask in his right hand,
those who make the request must prepare these two items.
The Commentary states:
"This is an exhortation to possess the essential causes, which is primarily intended for those with the capacity to respond.
The movement of the willow branch symbolizes wisdom."
Pure water, clear and still, symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The willow branch has two meanings:
first, the sense of brushing away and counteracting [impurities].
Second, "sweeping away" (vibhūta) corresponds to "subduing" (vinīta);
furthermore, "sweeping away" corresponds to "extinguishing.
Thus, the two—subduing and extinguishing—are equivalent.
Pure water also has two meanings:
first, the sense of washing away and counteracting;
second, the sense of awakening and subduing.
Furthermore, there are four meanings:
first, washing; second, moistening and soaking; third, awakening; and fourth, peace and happiness.
Washing corresponds to the "elimination" in the sense of destroying and extinguishing.
Moistening corresponds to elimination;
awakening corresponds to subduing;
and bliss corresponds to pacifying.
Furthermore, washing away, eliminating, and subduing toxic harms is the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*),
which through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) uproots suffering.
Saturating and moistening is the meaning of concentration (*samādhi*), which through great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness.
Awakening is the meaning of wisdom;
tranquility is the meaning of concentration.
This is with respect to ten types of practitioners.

Regarding each performing the *japa* (recitation) and so forth, etc.: Seventh, the Recitation of the Three Mantras. Regarding the recitation of the three mantras, the practitioner must first know the meaning of the mantras.
The Commentary states:
"The name 'mantra' (*dhāraṇī*) signifies a prayer of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), according to the analogy of the *mínglíng* (a type of wasp that nurtures caterpillars)."
It is also called "incantation" (vidyā).
This ritual method is entirely for the ten types of practitioners;
it is a secret technique corresponding with toxic harm that can effectively subdue those ten types of practitioners.
There are eight divisions:
first, those who undergo suffering; second, those who cultivate worldly goodness;
third, those who cultivate the path of the śrāvaka; fourth, those who cultivate the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The fifth is the cultivation of the six pāramitās, which is the path of practice.
The seventh is the cultivation of the distinct [teachings], and the eighth is the cultivation of the perfect [teaching].
There are two types of transformation and rebirth.
Distinguishing them from those at the thirty minds,
each stage from the first *bhūmi* of the Perfect Teaching upward possesses the poisonous harms of suffering, karma, craving, and views.
This is exactly as explained in the commentary (*śū*).
Furthermore, it says:
"The essence of this mantra is the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*)."
Neither empty nor existent, it obstructs the evil karma of the two extremes;
upholding the Middle Way, it is perfectly endowed with the three virtues.
Neither vertical nor horizontal, it is the inconceivable secret essence of all Buddhas.
It is further stated:
"Numinous wisdom, quiescently illuminating, takes the Dharma-body as its essence;
resonance and response constitute its school."
Its function is to rescue those in distress and uproot suffering;
by traversing the four teachings and ten dharma-realms, it eliminates the three obstacles.
One should know that the divine efficacy of this mantra is vast and far-reaching.
The *Zhiguan* states:
"The *Dhāraṇī for Eliminating and Subduing Poisonous Harm* can destroy karmic obstacles;
thus the people of Vaiśālī were restored to their original state."
The Dharani for Destroying Evil Karma can destroy karmic obstructions;
it purifies those who have violated the Brahma-conduct by cleansing away filth and impurities, causing them to attain purity.
The Six-Syllable Mantra Dharani can destroy the obstruction of afflictions.
One will undoubtedly attain the Buddha-way by purifying the roots of the three poisons.
According to the Commentary, the first mantra destroys afflictions (*kleśa*),
while the six-syllable mantra destroys retribution (*vipāka*).
Each has its own scriptural evidence;
for since each of the three mantras is capable of destroying the three respective obstacles,
they may all be discussed interchangeably.
Having gained a general understanding of the outline,
you should deliberate for yourself:
among these ten types of persons, in which position shall you direct your mind?
What obstacles do you wish to eliminate, and what goal do you seek to achieve?
Furthermore, in eliminating obstacles, one should apply the antidote to the most serious;
once the most serious is extinguished, the minor ones will follow suit and depart.
Rouse yourself with resolute diligence and do not harbor self-doubt;
how could the true Dharma-seal of the Buddhas of the three periods of time be anything other than authentic?
When you are about to recite the mantra:
First, kneel with one leg over the other and join the palms together with single-minded concentration.
Recite the names of the Triple Gem and Avalokiteśvara three times. The Commentary states:
"Reciting the Triple Gem three times symbolizes the removal of the three obstructions."
One should cause the various sounds to rise and fall in unison,
ensuring they do not become clamorous or distracting to the mind.
Namo buddhāya, namo dharmāya, namo saṃghāya.

Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Greatly Compassionate One of Great Renown who rescues and protects from suffering and distress. (Having recited this three times, one further chants:
"May you rescue me from my suffering and distress; Great Compassion covers all."
Universally emitting pure light, It extinguishes the darkness of ignorance;
To free them from the suffering of harm and poison, And from afflictions and all manner of diseases,
May they surely come to my presence And bestow upon me great peace and bliss.
I now prostrate in homage to the one whose very name rescues from calamity;
I now take refuge in the compassionate father of the world.
I pray that you will surely come to deliver me from the suffering of the three poisons.
"Grant me happiness in this present life, and [grant] great Nirvāṇa"—
thus it is said three times.
Of these four verses, the first two constitute the formal request.
Next are the two compilations.
Within the first, there are two parts.
The initial verse is a general request.
The following verse is a specific request.
The first verse consists of two parts;
the first line is a request made solely by oneself.
The subsequent three phrases apply to both oneself and others.
"Suffering and calamity" refers to the afflictions of the six sense organs.
"Enveloping all" applies universally to the ten realms.
"Universally emitting" refers to requesting the Great Wisdom Light to remove the darkness of ignorance.
Next, the individual requests specifically designate the three obstacles:
"poisonous harm" refers to the obstacle of suffering caused by karma.
The two obstacles are as stated in the text.
Great Bliss is nirvāṇa;
nirvāṇa is the three virtues (triguṇa).
The three virtues destroy the three obstacles.
The subsequent two lines conclude the request as in the text.
The meanings of "compassionate father" and so forth must be further investigated.
The Commentary states: For one who skillfully recites these four verses,
it serves as a condition for transforming obstacles and also as the foundation for entering into meditative observation in accordance with reality.
Therefore, it is necessary to have a brief understanding;
furthermore, each point must be discussed in relation to the ten types of practitioners.
From here on, the scriptural text praises the essence and function of the mantra.
While reciting, one should form the mental image of addressing the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
this divine mantra is certainly auspicious."
This is the Great Compassionate and Merciful Dharani Seal of all Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the past, present, and future.
Those who hear this mantra shall have all their sufferings forever exhausted.
May you always attain peace and happiness, remain far removed from the eight difficulties,
and achieve the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha so as to see the Buddhas before your eyes.
I shall now proclaim the divine mantra for protecting and saving sentient beings, spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Tadyathā | ūhaṇi | muhaṇi | dūbhaṇi | daṃbhaṇi | aṃdali | paṃdali | śaupeḍe | pampatārāre | vasiṇi | tadyathā | ili | mili | tiśule | kapale | khadiṃge | caṇḍālimāḍaṃge | rakṣa rakṣa sarvasattvān svāhā | tadyathā | gati gati | nigati | śrūvi śrūvi | rakṣa rakṣa sarvasattvān svāhā || The *Sūtra* states that after reciting this three or seven times, one should address the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
This divine mantra has been proclaimed by the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Those who recite and uphold this mantra...
They shall always be protected and sustained by all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas;
they shall be freed from fear and the harm of weapons, staves, and poisons,
as well as from diseases, thereby attaining freedom from affliction.
When these words were spoken, the people of Vaiśālī were restored to their original state. Having prostrated, they knelt again and descended as before.
Next, the *Pāpadeśanā-vighnavināśana-dhāraṇī* was recited.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and to protect all,
again entreated Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to proclaim a mantra for subduing and eliminating poisonous harms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
his heart permeated by great compassion and empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
spoke this dhāraṇī mantra for destroying evil karma and subduing poisonous harm.
Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha!
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One!
I only pray that you will have compassion for me and rescue me from my suffering;
likewise, rescue all sentient beings who are terrified and grant them great protection.

Tadyathā | dhāhani | mohani | dūbhani | dambhani | apakhye | mohiṣe | bhindali | bhaṇḍali | śubhite | bhaṇḍare | vasiṣṭhe | hulu hulu | bhindali | tulu tulu | bhaṇḍali | culu culu | nibhaṇḍali | dhu dhu | bhaṇḍaravasiṣṭhe | khine | kṣine | nikṣine | sarvāpāyakṣate | sarvavyūha-saṃstāga | apāyabhī | ridha | vidhyāna | svāhā | All fears, all poisons, and all harms.
When all evil spirits, tigers, wolves,
and lions hear this mantra,
their mouths will immediately be closed and they will be unable to cause harm.
If one who has violated the practice of the Brahma-faring commits the ten unwholesome karmas,
upon hearing this mantra,
they shall wash away their filth and impurities and regain purity.
Should one have karmic obstructions, turbid evil, or unwholesome states,
by invoking the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and reciting and upholding this mantra,
one will immediately break through those karmic obstructions and manifestly behold the Buddha.

Next, recite the six-syllable chapter-mantra *dhāraṇī*: *Namō buddhāya* | *Namō dharmāya* | *Namō saṃghāya* | *Namō śākyamunaye buddhāya* | *Namō avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya* | I shall now recite the Great Auspicious Six-Syllable Chapter-Mantra, the Divine Incantation for Saving from Suffering: *Tadyathā*: *Antali* | *Pantali* | *Kiyuli* | *Dantali* | *Śantali* | *Tiye-bhadra* | *Yaśa-bhadra* | *Paranirjivitsi* | *Nantali* | *Bhagali* | *Aruni* | *Phakuli* | *Mokuli* | *Dhupili* | *Svāhā*. At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken this divine incantation, [remained silent].
He addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If sons or daughters of good family among the fourfold assembly of disciples should hear the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara..."
Furthermore, one should receive, uphold, recite, and chant the six-syllable mantra.
Should one travel through a wilderness and lose one's way, [one shall not suffer].
By reciting this mantra,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, his great compassion permeating his heart, transforms himself into a human form,
shows them the way, and enables them to attain peace and security.
One will even attain great and wholesome benefits that subdue and eliminate poisonous harms;
all inauspicious matters of this life and future lives shall be forever exhausted without remainder.
One shall be fully endowed with morality, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇī.
8. Chapter Eight: Confession and Exposition. Having finished the mantra for confession and exposition, one should personally recollect former transgressions and give rise to great fear.
There has never been an evil karma that does not bring about a bitter retribution.
The Chan Gate says:
"The practitioner reflects."
If one's precepts are not pure, one must certainly repent.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Within the Buddha-dharma, there are two types of heroes."
First, one does not commit evil;
second, having committed it, one is able to repent.
One who recognizes their transgressions and repents is called a person of courage.
Now, "confession" (sānti) means to offer repentance and gratitude to the Triple Gem and to all sentient beings.
"Repentance" (hui) means to feel shame and remorse for one's transgressions, seeking mercy through the amendment of faults.
If these present sins of mine may be extinguished—
"In the future, I would rather lose my body and life than ever again commit such an offense.
As a bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"I would rather embrace this blazing great fire..."

I shall never dare to violate the pure precepts; these words below are from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Furthermore, I recall that although the nature of karma created since beginningless time until the present life is empty, its retribution is not lost.
Due to the causes and conditions of perversion, one gives rise to various grave offenses.
Shedding tears and weeping with sorrow, one should proclaim repentance aloud and mentally reflect:
"I and all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been constantly obstructed by the grave offenses of the three karmas and six sense faculties."
Failing to see the Buddhas, one does not know the essential path to liberation;
being subservient to birth and death, one does not understand the sublime principle.
Although I now know it, I am still the same as all sentient beings.
Obstructed by all manner of grave offenses,
we now, before Avalokiteśvara and the Buddhas of the ten directions,
universally take refuge and repent on behalf of all sentient beings.
I pray that you grant your protection so that all obstacles may be eliminated.
Having thus reflected, recite:
"May it be for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm."
Having chanted the confession for severing the three obstructions and taking refuge, one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and further reflects in the mind:
"From beginningless time until now, both I and all sentient beings, due to craving and false views,
have internally clung to a self and a person, and externally associated with evil friends."
They do not rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another's merit,
but instead extensively commit various transgressions through all three karmic gates;
though their actual deeds may not be numerous, their evil intent pervades them entirely.
Day and night they continue without interruption,
repeatedly concealing their transgressions so as not to let others know them;
they have no fear of the evil realms and lack both shame and remorse.
Because they formerly denied cause and effect, today they have deep faith in cause and effect;
they give rise to profound shame and remorse, they experience great fear,
and they confess their transgressions openly, severing the continuity of such thoughts.
Generate the bodhicitta, severing evil and cultivating goodness;
diligently exert yourself in the three karmas to overturn your past grave transgressions;
and rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of merit belonging to ordinary beings or sages alike.
One should contemplate that the Buddhas of the ten directions possess great merit and wisdom,
and are able to rescue and deliver oneself and all sentient beings,
placing them upon the shore of the three virtues from the sea of the two deaths.
Since beginningless time, not knowing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent,
they have extensively committed various evils;
now, knowing this emptiness and quiescence, they seek bodhi.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I have extensively cultivated all manner of goodness and universally severed all evils.
I pray that Avalokiteśvara will compassionately accept me.
With a sincere heart, I, Bhikṣu [Name], prostrate myself and repent.
I take refuge in the Triple Gem of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
and in our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha,
and all other Buddhas and holy sages who have been invited above.
The Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
out of pity and protection, has accepted my invitation;
he has manifested at this site of practice to accept my repentance.
The bhikṣus, such-and-such and the rest,
for the sake of all sentient beings submerged in the miserable realms throughout the dharma-realm,
have resolved their minds on bodhi and practice the path of the bodhisattvas.
However, because my three karmas and six sense faculties are burdened by many transgressions and the three obstructions are thick and heavy,
the practices and vows for bodhi cannot manifest before me.
Unable to benefit myself or others, I deeply reproach myself.
Today we respectfully invite all Buddhas and worthy sages,
including the Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and others,
to repent for our transgressions of the past, the present life, and future worlds.
All evil karma— through the three karmas and six sense faculties—
and the three obstructions and three poisons have been present since the beginning of one's own existence;
thus, one has wandered through the six realms of rebirth, assuming form in every place.
Lacking the eye of wisdom within and associating with evil people without,
they open the gates of negligence and create the karma of birth and death;
their branches, flowers, and leaves fill the three realms.
Among the twenty-five states of existence, there is none in which one does not undergo rebirth;
this cycle is boundless and its continuity is inexhaustible.
Having by chance obtained a human body, one may yet violate the various grave precepts.
Regarding all transgressions of the various sections of precepts, whether light or grave,
there are many instances of violation and opposition to the pure,
wondrous precepts of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
If one does not repent, one shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell,
or into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras; thereafter,
one will undergo immeasurable suffering among gods and humans.
Wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra, there is no time of liberation.
Today, having purified this sacred site,
I repent with a sincere heart and dare not conceal my transgressions.
I only pray that the Honored One, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
will manifest at this site of enlightenment and radiate supreme light,
touching our bodies and minds to bring them to purity.
Each and every root of the precepts shall be restored to its former state.
One shall cause the Three Jewels to flourish, giving rise to a mind that protects the Dharma, a mind that protects the precepts, and a mind of the four means of integration.
One shall give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and patience, as firm as a vajra.
I vow not to transgress again those offenses already committed.
Together with all sentient beings of the dharma realm, I repent them all.
Until the end of the future, may I always cultivate the practices and vows of bodhi.
In every lifetime they shall always dwell in pure Buddha-lands;
the three obstacles shall be forever eliminated, severing the three evil paths;
they shall eternally leave behind all suffering and achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
